title: Maze
alt: As a side effect of the research, mice are now the only known animals other than humans to have developed a Backrooms mythology.
transcript:
[A lab scene showing a large table on which is a maze, with walls about 3" (8 cm) high and open on the top so you can see the maze. Cueball, wearing a lab coat, is standing next to the table, looking at a small mouse that he is holding high in his right hand. Next to him is Megan, also in a lab coat, holding her left hand in the air and standing behind a podium as if speaking to an audience.]

[Caption below comic:]
Research breakthrough: After over a century of trials, scientists have finally found a mouse that can solve the maze.
explanation:
This comic references a common task used to benchmark cognitive functioning in mice, speed of maze-solving. For example, if testing whether XYZ compound impairs mouse spatial reasoning (or something like that), scientists might use the compound on n mice and not use the compound on n other mice, then compare the average maze-solving speed between the two groups. In such studies, the maze is designed to be solvable with one (or more) possible routes from the start point to the finish.

Supposedly, these 'scientists' have been using mice in mazes for over 100 years for the main purpose of finding a mouse that can solve the maze, and they are having a press conference because they finally found one. Having the mouse solve the maze is not usually the point of the experiment; the mouse's performance is simply a convenient benchmark to test some other experimental condition.

The title text references a fictional liminal space called , which is known for being infinite and maze-like. In 2026, the film  was released based on this "mythology". In this case, relative to a mouse, a moderately-sized maze for a human would be labyrinthian to a mouse, thereby creating the impression of an infinite maze. It is common for many human "mythologies" or stories to be based on a fear of the unknown, or on exaggerations or extrapolations of real fear-inducing phenomena; in this case the Backrooms are based on the unsettling phenomenon of liminal spaces and the familiar human fear of getting lost in an unfamiliar place. The title text implies that mice, because of their own experiences with mazes, have also developed their own Backrooms-like "mythology". Mice have not been known to do this in real life — yet.

This could also reference the popular book and film The Maze Runner, where a group of children are put into the center of a maze with no memory of who they are other than their names and must try to find a way out before they die (this could have been a much better explanation, but I don’t want to spoil anything for people who are or are going to read The Maze Runner).
